statements.label: supported
statements.text: Before neoadjuvant chemotherapy, tumor DNA was detected in 89% of urine supernatants and 85% of urine pellets, but in only 43% of plasma samples.
statements.evidence: We identified tumor DNA before NAC in 89% of urine supernatants, 85% of urine pellets, and 43% of plasma samples.
statements.note: The abstract reports pre-treatment tumor DNA detection in 89% of urine supernatants, 85% of urine pellets and 43% of plasma samples.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Patients with detectable plasma ctDNA before neoadjuvant chemotherapy more often had lymph node metastases at radical cystectomy.
statements.evidence: In plasma, detection of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) before NAC was associated with a lower NAC response rate (P < 0.001).
statements.note: The abstract links pre-treatment plasma ctDNA only to a lower chemotherapy response rate and reports nothing about lymph node findings at cystectomy.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Compared with plasma, urine supernatants and urine pellets both carried significantly higher levels of tumor DNA.
statements.evidence: Tumor DNA levels were higher in urine supernatants and urine pellets compared with plasma samples (P < 0.001).
statements.note: The abstract states that tumor DNA levels were higher in urine supernatants and urine pellets than in plasma samples (P < 0.001).

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Tumor DNA still detectable after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, whether in plasma, urine supernatant or urine pellet, was associated with poorer response rates.
statements.evidence: Detection of tumor DNA after NAC was associated with lower response rates in plasma, urine supernatant, and urine pellet (P < 0.001, P = 0.03, P = 0.002).
statements.note: The abstract reports that tumor DNA detected after chemotherapy was associated with lower response rates in all three sample types.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Patients identified by ctDNA testing alone as carrying BRCA or ATM alterations responded to PARP inhibitors as well as patients identified by tissue testing.
statements.evidence: We demonstrate that ctDNA can greatly complement tissue testing in identifying patients with mCRPC and BRCA or ATM alterations who are potentially suitable for receiving targeted PARP inhibitor treatments
statements.note: The abstract describes ctDNA-identified patients only as potentially suitable for PARP inhibitors and reports no treatment response data for any group.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Next-generation sequencing produced a result for 503 of the 619 ctDNA samples, a success rate of 81%.
statements.evidence: 81% (503/619) of ctDNA samples yielded an NGS result, of which 491 had a tumor tissue result.
statements.note: The abstract reports that 503 of 619 ctDNA samples (81%) yielded an NGS result.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Concordance between tissue and ctDNA was lower for homozygous deletions and large rearrangements than for nonsense, splice and frameshift alterations.
statements.evidence: At variant-subtype level, using tissue as reference, concordance was high for nonsense (93%), splice (87%), and frameshift (86%) alterations but lower for large rearrangements (63%) and homozygous deletions (27%)
statements.note: With tissue as reference, concordance was 86-93% for nonsense, splice and frameshift alterations but only 63% for large rearrangements and 27% for homozygous deletions.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Taking tissue as the reference, ctDNA matched 81% of tissue-positive and 92% of tissue-negative BRCA and ATM results.
statements.evidence: BRCA and ATM status in tissue compared with ctDNA showed 81% positive percentage agreement and 92% negative percentage agreement, using tissue as reference.
statements.note: The abstract reports 81% positive and 92% negative percentage agreement between tissue and ctDNA for BRCA and ATM status, with tissue as reference.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Of 41 patients with cancer of unknown primary, CUPiD made a prediction for 32, and 23 of 26 checkable predictions fit the subsequent or suspected primary diagnosis.
statements.evidence: In an additional cohort of 41 patients with CUP CUPiD predictions were made in 32/41 (78.0%) cases, with 88.5% of the predictions clinically consistent with a subsequent or suspected primary tumour diagnosis, when available (23/26 patients).
statements.note: The abstract reports predictions for 32 of 41 CUP patients, 88.5% (23/26) of them clinically consistent with a subsequent or suspected primary diagnosis where one was available.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In a test set of 143 cfDNA samples from 13 cancer types plus 27 non-cancer controls, CUPiD's tissue-of-origin accuracy was above 95%.
statements.evidence: We tested CUPiD on 143 cfDNA samples from patients with 13 cancer types alongside 27 non-cancer controls, with overall sensitivity of 84.6% and TOO accuracy of 96.8%.
statements.note: The abstract reports a tissue-of-origin accuracy of 96.8%, with 84.6% overall sensitivity, in this test set.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Pairing CUPiD with cfDNA mutation data pointed to possible diagnostic reclassification or changes of treatment for patients with cancer of unknown primary.
statements.evidence: Combining CUPiD with cfDNA mutation data demonstrated potential diagnosis re-classification and/or treatment change in this hard-to-treat cancer group.
statements.note: The abstract states that combining CUPiD with cfDNA mutation data showed potential diagnosis re-classification and/or treatment change in patients with CUP.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: CUPiD identified the tissue of origin more accurately than immunohistochemistry performed on tumour biopsies.
statements.evidence: Predicting tissue-of-origin (TOO) molecularly could help refine this diagnosis, with tissue acquisition barriers mitigated via liquid biopsies.
statements.note: The abstract reports CUPiD's own accuracy but never compares it with immunohistochemistry or any other tissue-based method.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In the GRAIL validation set, where every ctDNA fraction was under 0.05 and some were as low as 0.0003, cancer was separated from non-cancer with an AUC of 0.99.
statements.evidence: In the validation cohort where the ctDNA fractions were all <0.05 and as low as 0.0003, the cancer versus non-cancer area under the curve was 0.99.
statements.note: The abstract reports a cancer versus non-cancer AUC of 0.99 in the validation cohort whose ctDNA fractions were all below 0.05, down to 0.0003.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In the University of Wisconsin cohort, the classifier's accuracy was higher on the independent validation set than in cross-validated training.
statements.evidence: In the UW cohort, training cross-validated accuracy was 82.1%, and accuracy in the independent validation cohort was 86.6% despite a median ctDNA fraction of only 0.06.
statements.note: In the UW cohort, validation accuracy (86.6%) exceeded cross-validated training accuracy (82.1%), despite a median ctDNA fraction of 0.06.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Fragmentation analysis of targeted panel data classified tumor types more accurately than fragmentation analysis of whole-genome sequencing data.
statements.evidence: However, most of these analyses used whole-genome sequencing, which is insufficient to identify FDA-approved biomarker indications in a cost-effective manner.
statements.note: The abstract faults whole-genome sequencing only on cost and biomarker coverage and reports no accuracy comparison between targeted-panel and whole-genome fragmentation analysis.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: When the GRAIL cohort was split by ctDNA fraction, the model reached 80.6% cross-validated training accuracy and 76.3% accuracy on independent validation.
statements.evidence: In the GRAIL cohort, to assess how this approach performs in very low ctDNA fractions, training and independent validation were split based on ctDNA fraction. Training cross-validated accuracy was 80.6%, and accuracy in the independent validation cohort was 76.3%.
statements.note: For the GRAIL cohort, split by ctDNA fraction, the abstract reports 80.6% cross-validated training accuracy and 76.3% independent validation accuracy.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: The fragment-end model also determined which of the 11 cancer types each patient with cancer had.
statements.evidence: Using a combination of iwFAF and nine nucleotide frequencies from three positions surrounding fragment ends, we developed a machine learning model to differentiate healthy individuals from patients with cancer.
statements.note: The abstract describes the model only as separating healthy individuals from patients with cancer and reports no classification of cancer type.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The classifier built on iwFAF and fragment-end nucleotide frequencies detected cancer of any stage with an AUC of 0.91, and stage I cancer with an AUC of 0.87.
statements.evidence: We observed an area under the receiver operative characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.91 for detection of cancer at any stage and an AUC of 0.87 for detection of stage I cancer.
statements.note: The abstract reports AUCs of 0.91 for detecting cancer at any stage and 0.87 for stage I cancer.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The results held up even when only 1 million fragments were analysed per sample.
statements.evidence: Our findings remained robust with as few as 1 million fragments analyzed per sample
statements.note: The abstract states that the findings remained robust with as few as 1 million fragments analysed per sample.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The iwFAF metric was higher in cfDNA fragments that carried somatic mutations and correlated strongly with tumor fraction.
statements.evidence: We observed that iwFAF strongly correlated with tumor fraction, was higher for DNA fragments carrying somatic mutations, and was higher within genomic regions affected by copy number amplifications.
statements.note: The abstract reports that iwFAF correlated strongly with tumor fraction and was higher in fragments carrying somatic mutations and in amplified regions.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Three months after chemoradiation, 2-year progression-free survival was 24% for patients with dPCR-detectable HPV ctDNA, against 82% for those with undetectable HPV ctDNA.
statements.evidence: Patients with detectable HPV ctDNA on dPCR at the end of CRT, 4-6 weeks post-CRT, and 3 months post-CRT had significantly worse 2-year PFS compared with those with undetectable HPV ctDNA (77% v 51%, P = .03; 82% v 15%, P < .001; and 82% v 24%, P < .001, respectively)
statements.note: At 3 months post-CRT, 2-year PFS was 24% with detectable and 82% with undetectable HPV ctDNA on dPCR (P < .001).

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In multivariable models, inferior progression-free survival stayed independently tied to detectable HPV ctDNA, whether measured by dPCR or by HPV-seq.
statements.evidence: On multivariable analyses, detectable HPV ctDNA on dPCR and HPV-seq remained independently associated with inferior PFS.
statements.note: The abstract states that detectable HPV ctDNA on both dPCR and HPV-seq remained independently associated with inferior PFS in multivariable analyses.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Intensifying treatment for patients with persistent HPV ctDNA after chemoradiation improved their progression-free survival.
statements.evidence: HPV ctDNA testing can identify, as early as at the end of CRT, patients at high risk of recurrence for future treatment intensification trials.
statements.note: The abstract proposes HPV ctDNA for selecting patients for future intensification trials and reports no results of intensified treatment.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Measuring HPV ctDNA with the sequencing approach HPV-seq gave results similar to those obtained with digital PCR.
statements.evidence: HPV-seq showed similar results as dPCR.
statements.note: The abstract states that HPV-seq showed similar results to dPCR.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Offering this blood test in place of colonoscopy increased colorectal cancer screening uptake in the average-risk population.
statements.evidence: Blood-based screening offers the potential for higher adherence compared with endoscopy or stool-based testing but must first be clinically validated in a screening population.
statements.note: The abstract mentions only the potential for higher adherence; the study measured test accuracy against colonoscopy, not screening uptake.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The blood test detected 57 of 72 colorectal cancers (79.2%) and showed 91.5% specificity for advanced colorectal neoplasia.
statements.evidence: Sensitivity for colorectal cancer was 79.2% (57/72; 95% CI, 68.4%-86.9%) and specificity for advanced colorectal neoplasia was 91.5% (22 306/24 371; 95% CI, 91.2%-91.9%).
statements.note: The abstract reports 79.2% (57/72) sensitivity for colorectal cancer and 91.5% specificity for advanced colorectal neoplasia.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The blood test's sensitivity was lower for advanced precancerous lesions than for colorectal cancer.
statements.evidence: a blood-based test demonstrated acceptable accuracy for colorectal cancer detection, but detection of advanced precancerous lesions remains a challenge, and ongoing efforts are needed to improve test sensitivity
statements.note: Sensitivity was 12.5% for advanced precancerous lesions, short of its acceptance criterion, against 79.2% for colorectal cancer.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Only 15.5% of participants with a positive blood test had advanced colorectal neoplasia, whereas 90.8% of those testing negative were free of it.
statements.evidence: The negative predictive value for advanced colorectal neoplasia was 90.8% (22 306/24 567; 95% CI, 90.7%-90.9%) and the positive predictive value for advanced colorectal neoplasia was 15.5% (378/2443; 95% CI, 14.2%-16.8%).
statements.note: The abstract reports a positive predictive value of 15.5% and a negative predictive value of 90.8% for advanced colorectal neoplasia.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Patients with cancer showed region-specific frequencies of particular mutation types in tissue and cfDNA, and these patterns were associated with replication timing and chromatin features.
statements.evidence: found distinct regional mutation type-specific frequencies in tissue and cell-free DNA from patients with cancer that were associated with replication timing and other chromatin features
statements.note: The abstract reports distinct regional, mutation type-specific frequencies in tissue and cfDNA of cancer patients, associated with replication timing and other chromatin features.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Screening with the genome-wide mutational-profile model reduced lung cancer mortality in the prospective cohorts.
statements.evidence: This approach lays the groundwork for non-invasive cancer detection using genome-wide mutation features that may facilitate cancer screening and monitoring.
statements.note: The abstract presents screening as a future possibility and reports detection performance only, with no mortality outcomes.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: A machine-learning model of genome-wide mutational profiles plus other features, followed by CT imaging, detected over 90% of lung cancer patients, stage I and II included.
statements.evidence: A machine-learning model using genome-wide mutational profiles combined with other features and followed by CT imaging detected >90% of patients with lung cancer, including those with stage I and II disease.
statements.note: The abstract reports that the model followed by CT imaging detected more than 90% of patients with lung cancer, including stage I and II disease.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In an independent validation cohort, the fixed model flagged patients with cancer earlier than standard approaches did.
statements.evidence: The fixed model was validated in an independent cohort, detected patients with cancer earlier than standard approaches and could be used to monitor response to therapy.
statements.note: The abstract states that, in an independent cohort, the fixed model detected patients with cancer earlier than standard approaches.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In over 60% of lumbar-puncture CSF samples, tumor DNA sufficed to test IDH and TERT promoter mutations, EGFR amplification, CDKN2A/B deletion and MGMT methylation.
statements.evidence: Nevertheless, in >60% of LP CSF samples, tumor DNA is sufficient to assess a selected panel of genetic alterations (IDH and TERT promoter mutations, EGFR amplification, CDKN2A/B deletion: ITEC protocol) and MGMT methylation
statements.note: The abstract reports that in more than 60% of LP CSF samples tumor DNA was sufficient for the ITEC panel and MGMT methylation.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: CSF obtained by lumbar puncture contained lower levels of tumor DNA than CSF collected close to the tumor.
statements.evidence: We report that tumor DNA is abundant in CSF close to the tumor, but scanty and mostly below NGS sensitivity threshold in CSF from LP.
statements.note: The abstract reports abundant tumor DNA in CSF close to the tumor but scanty amounts, mostly below NGS sensitivity, in CSF from lumbar puncture.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Tumor DNA in CSF comes mainly from cells invading the liquoral spaces, which creates a gradient that fades with distance from the tumor.
statements.evidence: Indeed, tumor DNA is mostly released by cells invading liquoral spaces, generating a gradient that attenuates by departing from the tumor.
statements.note: The abstract states that tumor DNA is mostly released by cells invading liquoral spaces, producing a gradient that attenuates away from the tumor.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Glioma molecular subtypes determined from lumbar-puncture CSF predicted overall survival of the newly diagnosed patients.
statements.evidence: This study shows potentialities and limitations of CSF liquid biopsy in achieving molecular characterization of gliomas at first clinical presentation and proposes a protocol to maximize diagnostic information retrievable from CSF DNA.
statements.note: The abstract concerns molecular characterization and diagnosis from CSF DNA and reports no survival or other outcome data.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Patients whose ctDNA was still detectable after 4 weeks of first-line ARPI treatment had the shortest progression-free and overall survival, independent of clinical prognostic factors.
statements.evidence: PFS and OS were shortest for patients with persistent ctDNA at 4 weeks (univariate HR, 4.79; 95% CI, 2.62-8.77 and univariate HR, 5.49; 95% CI, 2.76-10.91, respectively), independent of clinical prognostic factors.
statements.note: The abstract reports that PFS and OS were shortest for patients with persistent ctDNA at 4 weeks, independent of clinical prognostic factors.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Switching patients with persistent ctDNA at 4 weeks to a different therapy prolonged their survival.
statements.evidence: Early changes in ctDNA fraction are strongly linked to duration of first-line ARPI treatment benefit and survival in mCRPC and may inform early therapy switches or treatment intensification.
statements.note: The abstract suggests ctDNA changes may inform early therapy switches but reports no outcomes of switching treatment.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Among 81 patients with mCRPC, ctDNA was detectable in 59% of baseline samples but in only 36% of samples taken after 4 weeks of ARPI treatment.
statements.evidence: ctDNA was detected in 48/81 (59%) baseline and 29/81 (36%) 4-week samples.
statements.note: The abstract reports ctDNA detection in 48/81 (59%) baseline and 29/81 (36%) 4-week samples.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In samples with detectable ctDNA, the median ctDNA fraction was lower after 4 weeks of ARPI treatment than at baseline.
statements.evidence: ctDNA fraction for samples with detected ctDNA was lower at 4 weeks versus baseline (median 5.0% versus 14.5%, P = 0.017).
statements.note: Among samples with detected ctDNA, the median ctDNA fraction fell from 14.5% at baseline to 5.0% at 4 weeks (P = 0.017).
